stops.name: Berlin, the Travel Diary appears
stops.campa: In 1919 the Reisetagebuch eines Philosophen is published at last, and defeated Germany falls on it as on bread. The book written before the catastrophe reads as the map out of it: fifty thousand copies, edition after edition, a nation locked inside its borders travelling the earth by lamplight. Overnight the landless Baltic count is the most famous philosopher in the German tongue. Letters arrive by the sack. The tradition records the wonder plainly: the war buried the book for seven years, and the burial made it scripture.

stops.name: Darmstadt, founding of the School of Wisdom
stops.campa: In November 1920, under the patronage of Ernst Ludwig, Grand Duke of Hesse, and with the publisher Otto Reichl, Keyserling opens the Schule der Weisheit at Darmstadt. In a Germany stripped of thrones and certainties, a courtyard of the spirit: not a university, for it examines no one; not a church, for it converts no one. Its purpose is Sinneserfassung: the seizing of meaning, and its method the orchestra: the best minds of the age summoned yearly to sound a single theme together. The dispossessed aristocrat has built himself a duchy of wisdom.

stops.name: Darmstadt, the Tagore week
stops.campa: From 9 to 14 June 1921 Rabindranath Tagore comes to Darmstadt, and the School of Wisdom holds its Tagore-Woche. The poet whom Keyserling first sought out in Calcutta during the world journey now sits in a Hessian garden while thousands gather on the lawns to hear the East speak to the beaten West. Tagore reads, the crowd stands silent under the June trees, and for one week a provincial German residence city is the meeting-point of the hemispheres. The congresses that follow draw Jung, Scheler, Driesch, Frobenius, Richard Wilhelm: the orchestra assembling year by year.

stops.name: Darmstadt, Jung at the congress of Man and Earth
stops.campa: At the school's congress on Mensch und Erde, Carl Gustav Jung lectures on the earth-conditioning of the psyche: the soul as a creature of landscape, climate and soil. Keyserling and Jung, allies and sparring partners, are building between them the instruments this itinerary itself is made of: the idea that continents have souls and souls have continents. The yearbook Der Leuchter carries the lectures out into the world. In the Darmstadt halls the twenties burn at their brightest; no one present knows how few years the light has left.

stops.name: New York, the American lecture tour
stops.campa: Through the twenties the philosopher of Darmstadt becomes a planetary lecturer, and America receives him like a touring virtuoso: packed halls, headlines, hostesses at war over his evenings. He crosses the continent dissecting it in public, the young civilisation of pure becoming, gathering the material of America Set Free. He plays the celebrity and despises the machinery of celebrity, and does both at the top of his voice. The Old World's wisdom, sold out in the New: the tradition notes the irony and the triumph together.

stops.name: Versailles, the Hôtel des Réservoirs
stops.campa: In the first days of January 1929, in the freezing Hôtel des Réservoirs beside the park of Versailles, Keyserling at last meets Victoria Ocampo, the Argentine who has been writing to him for two years and has summoned him across the ocean. The canon carries both testaments of the encounter and they contradict each other absolutely: he arrives certain she has given herself to him in the spirit; she arrives to meet a mind and finds a minotaur. The delirium of Versailles, mutual, magnificent, humiliating, becomes the wound through which South America will enter his philosophy.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the landing on the third day of creation
stops.campa: In the southern winter of 1929 he lands at Buenos Aires for the lecture tour arranged under Ocampo's patronage and the Amigos del Arte. From the first hours the continent works on him below the mind: a heavy, cold, ancient influence rising through the pavement itself. The canon names the revelation: this is the continent of the third day of creation, where life has not yet fully consented to spirit: the world of the serpent, of blood, of primordial fear. The halls fill for his lectures; underneath, the Meditations have already begun.
stops.quote_source: Südamerikanische Meditationen (1932), title of the first meditation

stops.name: San Isidro, Villa Ocampo and the Delirio
stops.campa: At San Isidro, in the villa above the río de la Plata, the drama of Versailles is played out to its end. Ocampo lodges him grandly and refuses him herself; the philosopher rages like a natural force misdirected; between them stands the misunderstanding that neither will ever fully forgive nor fully regret. The canon keeps both books: his memoir naming her the woman who was everything, hers naming him the traveller and one of his shadows; and the tradition rules that both are true. Out of the wreck each builds a monument: she the review Sur, he the Meditations.

stops.name: The pampa, the estancia night
stops.campa: He is taken out onto the pampa, and the plain finishes what the city began. Land without limit and without feature, cattle moving like slow weather, the gaucho silent under a sky that does not explain itself. Here he first isolates the continent's ruling force and gives it its Spanish name: gana, the dark craving that precedes and outranks the will, the pull of the blood that says I feel like it or I do not, and needs no reason. Europe wills; South America has gana. The philosopher feels it rising in his own veins like groundwater.
stops.quote_source: Südamerikanische Meditationen (1932), meditation VII, 'Gana', the formula of the continent

stops.name: Santiago de Chile, across the Andes
stops.campa: The trans-Andean railway lifts him over the cordillera past Aconcagua, stone heaped on stone to the ceiling of the hemisphere, and drops him into Santiago. Chile shows him the continent's other face: a hard, seismic land where the earth itself keeps la gana: trembling when it feels like it, killing when it feels like it. He lectures; the republic's élite fills the halls; and the Meditations gain their chapters on primordial fear, on the reptile cold beneath American life, on delicadeza: the exquisite courtesy that men build as a dyke against the abyss.

stops.name: The altiplano, the cold of the reptile
stops.campa: Northward onto the Bolivian altiplano, four thousand metres of thin blue air between Titicaca and the volcanoes. The puna seizes his lungs and his metaphysics at once: on this oldest of inhabited deserts, among Aymara herders whose faces keep the stillness of the pre-human, he touches the stratum he has been descending toward since Buenos Aires: the third day of creation itself, life still cold, still bound, obedience without freedom. The reptile, the blood, the mineral patience of the Indian: the Meditations receive their deepest and darkest pages here, at the roof of the dispossessed world.

stops.name: La Paz, doctor honoris causa
stops.campa: In La Paz, the city poured into its canyon beneath Illimani, the university makes him doctor honoris causa in 1929, the altiplano crowning the traveller who has just declared it the primordial floor of the human world. He accepts the laurel gasping in the altitude, half ironic, half moved: the continent of gana bestowing, when it feels like it, its highest honour on the man who named its craving. It is the outermost point of the journey; from here the road turns home, and the harvest turns inward.
